---
title: "Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)"
format: html
---

<!-- Supp: Agents track. System-level pattern, not model-specific. -->

::: {.callout-tip title="TL;DR" icon="false"}
**RAG** augments a generative model with a retrieval step: relevant
documents are fetched from an external store at inference time and added
to the context. The model's weights stay fixed; knowledge lives in the
retrieval index, not the parameters.
:::

**Depends on:** [Agent Architectures Overview](00_overview.qmd) · [Alignment & Instruction Tuning](../../02_transformer/07_alignment.qmd) (RAG as a fix for stale, parametric knowledge)

## Why this matters

[Alignment & Instruction Tuning](../../02_transformer/07_alignment.qmd)
already introduced *why* RAG exists: a pretrained model's knowledge is
frozen at training time and hallucinates confidently when asked about
anything newer or more specific than its training data covered. This note
goes one level deeper, into the retrieval **pipeline** itself: how a query
actually becomes retrieved text, and the specific failure modes and fixes
that pipeline has accumulated.

## The mechanism

A RAG system runs four stages before generation even starts, and the
retrieved text is then just concatenated into the model's context
alongside the query.

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 620 140" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
     style="font-family:system-ui,sans-serif;max-width:600px;display:block;margin:1.5rem auto">
  <defs>
    <marker id="rag-ah" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="6" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto">
      <polygon points="0,0 8,3 0,6" fill="#7c3aed"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <rect x="10"  y="45" width="90" height="50" rx="6" fill="#fef9c3" stroke="#eab308"/>
  <text x="55" y="75" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#854d0e">Query</text>

  <rect x="130" y="45" width="90" height="50" rx="6" fill="#ede9fe" stroke="#7c3aed"/>
  <text x="175" y="75" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#5b21b6">Embed</text>

  <rect x="250" y="45" width="90" height="50" rx="6" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#3b82f6"/>
  <text x="295" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="#1e40af">Vector</text>
  <text x="295" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="#1e40af">index</text>

  <rect x="370" y="45" width="90" height="50" rx="6" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#22c55e"/>
  <text x="415" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="#166534">Top-k</text>
  <text x="415" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="#166534">rerank</text>

  <rect x="490" y="45" width="120" height="50" rx="6" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#eab308"/>
  <text x="550" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="#854d0e">Context + query</text>
  <text x="550" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="#854d0e">→ generation</text>

  <line x1="100" y1="70" x2="128" y2="70" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#rag-ah)"/>
  <line x1="220" y1="70" x2="248" y2="70" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#rag-ah)"/>
  <line x1="340" y1="70" x2="368" y2="70" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#rag-ah)"/>
  <line x1="460" y1="70" x2="488" y2="70" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#rag-ah)"/>
</svg>
```

- **Embed**: documents (and later, the query) are mapped to dense vectors
  by an embedding model, the same idea as the contrastive encoders in
  [Self-Supervised Learning](../self_supervised.qmd) or CLIP's text tower.
- **Index**: document vectors are stored in a vector database that
  supports fast nearest-neighbor search over millions of entries.
- **Query**: the user's query is embedded with the same model, and the
  index returns the $k$ nearest document vectors.
- **Rerank**: a smaller, more expensive model re-scores the top-$k$
  candidates for relevance, since fast approximate nearest-neighbor search
  trades some precision for speed.

### Chunking and embedding choices

Documents are split into **chunks** before embedding, since a single
vector cannot represent an entire long document precisely. Chunk size is a
direct tradeoff: smaller chunks retrieve more precisely but lose
surrounding context; larger chunks preserve context but dilute the
embedding with irrelevant content. The embedding model itself is usually a
contrastively-trained encoder, the same family as
[SimCLR/MoCo](../self_supervised.qmd), applied to text instead of images.

### Naive RAG vs. advanced RAG

The pipeline above, embed the query once and retrieve once, is **naive
RAG**, and it fails when the query itself is a poor search term for what's
actually needed. Two refinements address this directly.

- **HyDE** [@gao2023hyde]: instead of embedding the raw query, first ask
  the language model to generate a *hypothetical answer*, then embed and
  search with that hypothetical document. A generated answer is closer, in
  embedding space, to the real answer documents than the original question
  is.
- **FLARE** [@jiang2023flare]: instead of retrieving once up front,
  retrieve **actively**, mid-generation, whenever the model's own
  confidence in its next tokens drops, triggering a fresh retrieval query
  at exactly the point new information is needed.

### What to observe

- Every stage of the pipeline (embed, index, query, rerank) is a place
  quality can be lost; RAG's overall quality is bounded by its weakest
  stage, usually retrieval, not generation.
- HyDE and FLARE both attack the same weakness, a naive query is often not
  what should be searched for, from different angles: rewrite the query,
  or retrieve at a better time.
- RAG requires no change to the underlying model's weights, the direct
  contrast to fine-tuning: knowledge is added by changing what's *in the
  index*, not what's in the parameters.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: RAG's latency is not free" icon="false"}
Every retrieval step adds a round-trip to the vector index before
generation can proceed; FLARE's repeated mid-generation retrieval trades
that latency for freshness, and is only worth it when generation quality
would otherwise suffer from stale context.
:::

## Application & impact

| Concept here | What it became | Where you see it today |
|---|---|---|
| Embed → index → query → rerank | The standard RAG pipeline | Nearly every production LLM application with private or fresh data |
| HyDE's query rewriting | Bridging the query-document embedding gap | Common preprocessing step in RAG pipelines |
| FLARE's active retrieval | Retrieval as part of the agent loop, not a one-shot step | Agentic RAG systems |

::: {.callout-note title="Key takeaway" icon="false"}
RAG decouples knowledge from weights by adding a retrieval pipeline in
front of generation. The pipeline mechanics, chunking, embedding, and when
to retrieve, are where most of RAG's practical quality is won or lost, not
in the generation step itself.
:::
